title: Pure Function
body:
A function is **pure** when it returns the same result for the same arguments and changes
nothing else. Two clauses, and both are load-bearing: the first rules out reading hidden
state, the second rules out writing it.

```haskell
add :: Int -> Int -> Int
add x y = x + y            -- pure: depends on nothing else, changes nothing
```

```c
int counter = 0;
int next(void) { return ++counter; }   /* impure both ways: reads and writes a global */
```

`next()` is the whole problem in four characters. Called twice it gives two answers, so it is
not a function in the mathematical sense at all, and none of the reasoning below applies to it.

## Referential transparency

The property purity buys: **an expression may be replaced by its value without changing the
program's meaning.** If `f 3` is `7`, then every `f 3` in the program is `7`, and you may
substitute one for the other freely. That is exactly beta reduction from [[Lambda Calculus]],
promoted from a proof technique to a fact about real code.

Three things fall out of it, and they are the practical payoff:

| You may | Because |
|---|---|
| **reorder** two calls | neither can observe the other having run |
| **cache** a result (memoise) | the answer cannot have changed since last time |
| **run calls in parallel** | there is no shared mutable state to race over |

That third row is the strongest argument the paradigm has. Every lock note in
[[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] ([[Mutex Lock]], [[Spin Lock]], [[Semaphores]]) exists to protect a
[[Synchronization\|critical section]], and a critical section is a piece of shared mutable
state. Pure code has none, so it has no races to prevent and no [[Critical Section]] to
lock. See [[Immutability]] for the data-side half of the same argument.

Referential transparency is also what makes [[Program Correctness]] tractable: you can reason
about a Haskell program by substituting equals for equals, the way you would simplify an
algebraic expression, which you categorically cannot do with `next()` above.

## But programs have to do something

A program that changes nothing outside itself also prints nothing, reads no files, and is
useless. The trick is not to abolish effects but to **make them values**: an `IO a` is a
*description* of an effect, built and combined purely, and only the runtime performs it. That
is [[Monadic IO]], and it is why [[Monad]] is not an academic detour in this course.

[[Void]] (COMP 3612) is the sharpest anti-example the vault has: a `void` function returns
nothing, so the only reason to call it is a side effect. It is the exact shape of function
this paradigm says should not exist.

## Core Facts to Know

- Pure: same input gives same output, **and** nothing else changes.
- Both clauses matter; reading a global breaks purity just as writing one does.
- **Referential transparency**: an expression may be replaced by its value.
- It licenses reordering, caching, and parallelism without further proof.
- It is beta reduction from [[Lambda Calculus]] applied to real programs.
- Pure code has no shared mutable state, so it has no data races and needs no locks.
- Effects are not banned; they are made into values (`IO a`) and performed by the runtime.
- A `void`-returning function is pure only if it does nothing at all.
